topic: Decision Making to Improve Human Resource Performance
subject: business-studies

items.title: The Hawthorne effect is real but smaller than the textbook story
items.claim: Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies (1927-32) are taught as showing that worker productivity rose because of attention paid to them. What does re-analysis of the original data show?

options.text: The effect was even larger than originally reported

Levitt and List's 2011 re-analysis of original records suggests the 'Hawthorne effect' was much weaker than reported; productivity gains were largely explained by which workers were replaced and the Monday rebound after weekends
No data from the studies survived
The lighting reduction was actually the cause

items.reveal:
Steven Levitt and John List (American Economic Journal, 2011) accessed original Hawthorne Works data digitised by the University of Wisconsin. They found the famous 'productivity rose whatever you changed' pattern was much weaker than Mayo claimed and largely artifactual.

The broader 'human relations' school it spawned remained influential — but the founding evidence base was weaker than generations of textbooks suggested.
items.why: Iconic findings get retold long after the evidence has been challenged. Modern HR theory survives, but its founding study should be taught with caveats.

items.title: Brand value can exceed half of market capitalisation
items.claim: Interbrand's 2023 Best Global Brands ranking valued Apple's brand at around $502 billion. What's the relationship between brand value and accounting?

options.text: Brand value appears directly on the balance sheet for all firms
Under IFRS / UK GAAP, internally generated brands are not recognised as balance sheet assets; purchased brands can be. Apple's $502bn estimate is an external valuation, not a reported figure
Brand value equals market cap minus debt
Brand value has no relationship with share price

items.reveal:
IAS 38 prohibits capitalising internally generated brands; accounting wants to avoid the manipulability of self-assessed intangibles. Acquired brands (e.g. Cadbury bought by Kraft for £11.5bn in 2010) appear at acquisition cost as 'goodwill' or identified intangibles.

Interbrand, Kantar BrandZ and Brand Finance use different methodologies — discounted cash flow from brand-attributable earnings — and produce different rankings. The numbers are estimates, but the underlying point is real: a meaningful share of S&P 500 market value sits in intangibles invisible on balance sheets.
items.why: Investors price intangibles even when accountants don't book them. The gap between book and market value for brand-heavy firms is largely brand and goodwill.
